chapters.title: Chapter 4: Nudges and Public Policy in India

lessons.title: Tax Filing and Compliance: Nudging Indians Toward Honest Disclosure

children.text: "Dear Taxpayer, file your ITR before 31st July to avoid last-minute rush and penalty." You've likely received a version of this SMS every July. It looks like a simple reminder. Look closer and it's doing at least two things this course has already named: reminding you, and quietly framing the deadline as an avoidable loss rather than a neutral date. Tax compliance is one of the purest testing grounds for nudges anywhere in government, because the desired behavior, honest, timely disclosure, is precisely measurable, and every percentage point of improvement has a known revenue value. This closing lesson of Chapter 4 traces how many of this course's ideas converge on a single tax return.

body.text: Governments no longer have to guess whether a nudge works on taxpayers. Tax authorities run genuine randomized field experiments on reminder wording, because the revenue stakes justify the rigor, and the results have repeatedly shown that how compliance is framed changes how much of it you get, often more cheaply than adding enforcement staff.

children.text: The Classic Field Experiment: "Most People Pay Their Tax on Time"

The UK's Behavioural Insights Team, the world's first government nudge unit from Chapter 1, ran one of its best-known field trials directly with HM Revenue and Customs. Researchers Michael Hallsworth, John List, Robert Metcalfe, and Ivo Vlaev tested reminder letters sent to taxpayers who hadn't yet paid. Some letters simply restated the amount owed. Others added a single descriptive-norm sentence, close to "nine out of ten people in the UK pay their tax on time," the same descriptive-norm mechanism from the previous lesson's hotel towel study. The social-norm letters measurably increased the share of recipients who paid promptly, and because the trial ran across a large national taxpayer pool, even a modest percentage-point improvement translated into a meaningful amount of additional revenue collected purely from changing a sentence, with no change to the tax owed or the penalty for non-payment.
India's Version: Pre-Filled Forms, and a Default That Changed Overnight

markDefs.definition: A comprehensive statement introduced by the CBDT, pre-filling an Income Tax Return with salary, TDS, interest, dividend, and capital gains data already reported to the tax department by employers, banks, and other institutions.

children.text: India runs its own version of this at the point of filing itself. The

pre-fills a taxpayer's return with income already reported to the department by employers, banks, and registrars, the same friction-removal nudge behind UPI's QR code in the last lesson, applied to a tax form instead of a payment. And Budget 2023 made the concessional new tax regime under Section 115BAC of the Income-tax Act, 1961, the default regime for individual taxpayers from FY 2023-24 onward, with the older regime now requiring an active opt-in each year. This is the single largest default-effect policy change in recent Indian tax history, run through the exact mechanism Chapter 2 covered for EPF contribution rates: whichever option requires no action from the taxpayer is the option most taxpayers will end up with.
TDS: The Tax You Never Feel Yourself Losing

Most salaried tax in India is never paid by the taxpayer at all, in the felt sense. Tax Deducted at Source removes it from a salary before it ever reaches an employee's account, which means two ideas from Chapter 2 apply at once: there is no pain-of-paying moment, since the money was never decoupled from the employer to the employee in the first place, and there is no endowment-effect resistance either, since you cannot feel you're losing something you never possessed as yours. This is very likely part of why withholding-based tax systems achieve dramatically higher voluntary compliance than systems that ask people to pay a lump sum from money they've already felt as their own.

body.text: Behavioral economists have long pointed to a related pattern: many taxpayers who receive a large refund, because TDS across multiple employers or income sources was conservatively estimated, treat it almost like a bonus, even though it's really an interest-free loan they extended to the government all year. A rupee never felt as "yours" is a rupee whose absence, and eventual return, both feel different from ordinary spending or saving.

body.title: Price the interest-free loan
body.prompt: A taxpayer's TDS deductions across the year exceed their actual tax liability by ₹40,000. The refund takes 6 months to arrive. If they could otherwise have earned 6% per annum on that money in a savings account, how much interest income did they forgo?
body.explanation: ₹40,000 × 6% × (6 ÷ 12) = ₹1,200. The refund itself feels like a windfall, but the taxpayer effectively lent the government ₹40,000 for six months at 0% interest, a real, if usually invisible, cost of over-withholding.

children.text: Which brings us back to the SMS this lesson opened with. "Avoid last-minute rush and penalty" is loss framing from Chapter 3, applied to a filing deadline instead of a negotiation: it frames filing late as losing money you'd otherwise keep, via the late-filing fee under Section 234F of the Income-tax Act, 1961, rather than framing early filing as a gain. A reminder alone is a nudge from Chapter 1's original taxonomy, nothing is banned or repriced by sending it. The specific wording choice, loss-framed rather than gain-framed, is the same deliberate lever Chapter 3 covered for negotiation, now aimed at a national compliance deadline instead of a single deal.

body.title: Choosing the right nudge for the right segment
body.scenario: A state tax department wants to improve on-time professional tax filing among small business owners. Internal data shows 80% of this group already files on time, but the remaining 20% consistently files late every year despite receiving standard reminder SMS messages.
body.prompt: Given everything covered in Chapter 4, what nudge would you recommend testing, and what would you specifically want to check before rolling it out widely?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Since 80% already comply, a descriptive norm message, close to "4 out of 5 business owners in your district file on time," is safe to use here without boomerang risk, unlike the ward-level waste segregation example earlier in this chapter where the true compliance rate was too low to state plainly.
2. Given that standard reminders have already been tried on the remaining 20% without success, it's worth testing whether the issue is really about reminder timing or wording at all, versus a genuine friction problem, similar to how UPI needed Zero MDR, not friction removal alone, to fully work for merchants.
3. A reasonable test would compare the existing standard reminder against a version adding both the descriptive norm and an explicit, specific Section 234F loss-framed penalty amount, run as a genuine randomized trial across the late-filing segment rather than rolled out to everyone at once.
4. Before scaling any result, the department should check whether the 20% persistent late-filers share a common underlying cause, like a specific business type, all currently switched from an old accounting default, or seasonal cash-flow timing, since a nudge fixes friction and framing, not a structural reason someone can't file on time.

body.title: Which mechanism, across the whole course?
body.question: A salaried employee says, "I never really notice paying income tax, it's just gone before I see my salary, but I definitely notice writing a cheque for my professional tax once a year." Which two concepts from this course best explain the difference in how these two payments feel?
options: Payment decoupling and the endowment effect
The availability heuristic and present bias
The decoy effect and choice overload
body.explanation: TDS is decoupled, deducted automatically before the money is ever felt as the employee's own, and because it was never possessed, the endowment effect never applies to it either. The annual cheque, by contrast, is a direct, undecoupled payment of money already felt as owned, which is exactly why it registers far more sharply.

body.title: Name the deduction mechanism
body.textWithBlank: Removing income tax from a salary automatically, before an employee ever receives or feels ownership of that money, is called Tax Deducted at ___.
body.explanation: TDS is a structural application of payment decoupling from Chapter 2: because the money is never felt as the taxpayer's own, neither the pain of paying nor the endowment effect ever gets a chance to apply to it.

body.title: Did the UK's tax nudge letters really move the needle at national scale?

children.text: The Hallsworth, List, Metcalfe, and Vlaev study, published in 2017 in the Journal of Public Economics, is one of the most cited field experiments in behavioral public finance precisely because HMRC ran it as a genuine randomized controlled trial across real taxpayers owing real money, not a lab simulation. The finding held up under replication interest and directly shaped how several other countries' tax authorities, and later India's own compliance messaging, approached reminder design: treat the exact wording of a compliance nudge as an empirical, testable question, not a communications afterthought.

body.label: When the new tax regime became the default
body.context: Budget 2023 made the concessional regime under Section 115BAC the default for individual taxpayers, requiring an active opt-in to use the older regime instead.

cards.definition: A pre-filled statement of a taxpayer's reported income, used to reduce the friction and error rate of filing an ITR.
Since FY 2023-24, the concessional tax regime under Section 115BAC applies automatically unless a taxpayer actively opts for the older regime, a national-scale application of the default effect.
Tax withheld from income before the recipient ever possesses it, combining payment decoupling and the absence of the endowment effect to reduce the felt cost of paying tax.
The Income-tax Act, 1961 provision imposing a late-filing fee, commonly used as the loss-framed consequence cited in filing-deadline reminder messages.
A randomized trial testing different reminder or messaging wording on real taxpayers, pioneered at scale by the UK's Behavioural Insights Team with HMRC.

points: Tax authorities run genuine randomized field experiments on nudge wording, and the UK's HMRC trial found a simple descriptive-norm sentence measurably increased on-time payment across a large national taxpayer pool.
India's AIS pre-fills ITR data as a friction-removal nudge, while the new tax regime becoming the default from FY 2023-24 is a national-scale application of the default effect from Chapter 2.

TDS combines payment decoupling and the absence of the endowment effect, which is very likely part of why withholding-based tax systems achieve markedly higher voluntary compliance than lump-sum payment systems.
Deadline reminders citing a specific penalty, like Section 234F, use loss framing from Chapter 3, the same deliberate lever covered for negotiation, now aimed at a filing date instead of a deal.

This closes Chapter 4's throughline: PMJDY's defaults, UPI's friction removal, Swachh Bharat's social norms, and tax filing's reminders and decoupling are the same handful of mechanisms from Chapters 1 through 3, simply deployed by the state rather than a business. Chapter 5 turns to where these same mechanisms show up inside organizations and the workplace.
